utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you. Can you follow in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager, good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good morning to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, David Cunningham with Aleksandar Vujic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning to you. First of all our apologies for starting a quarter of an hour a late but we were discussing the latest motion by Mr. Ackerman. In fact I do not see Mr. Ackerman present here. We require his presence at some point in time today. He chooses the time, whether it will be just after the first break or after the second break or at the end of the sitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I will call him at the next break and tell him, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. That's unless he withdraws the motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'll call him and he'll be here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can also tell him that we are not exactly happy with it and that's why we want him present here because we don't fancy at all, Mr. Cunningham, giving the public the wrong impression that there is some sort of an unfair trial going on and that the Defence is being deprived of the chances of providing -- of having a fair trial for the client. And that's when we hit back. So Mr. Ackerman be better prepared. He knows exactly where we stand and he knows exactly why we stand where we stand. Secondly, there is also another thing that I want to add in addition to the order that we made yesterday through the Registrar relating to Mr. Brdjanin's motion of the 23rd of July for the Registrar to provide certain documents. Let's go into private session for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: That preliminary matter is whether or not the Defence would withdraw those objections to the Petrovac exhibits that had been previously raised, and much as I told the Court yesterday, the objection remains.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So Ms. Korner, you know exactly now how to proceed. You will not in any way find any obstructions on our side. It's unfortunate but if you can find a method which will reduce, economise on time it will be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. I may say that it's my view that counsel do owe a duty to the Court as well, not to waste unnecessary time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But -- however, I've taken the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, judge and my apologies to you for keeping you waiting but we had a preliminary matter, procedural, that does not concern you and which we had to discuss first in conference and then here. And that kept us from starting on time as scheduled. Please may I ask you to re-enter your solemn declaration, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, judge. Please take a chair and Ms. Korner will --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Judge, good morning, can I ask one further question, please, on the topic that we were dealing with yesterday which was the change of street names and the like? Did there come a time when the name of the municipality was changed, in other words -- can you hear?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. That -- from becoming -- from being called Bosanski Petrovac, it became known as, I think, just Petrovac; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you roughly tell us when that happened?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it happened whether the former half of 1993 or towards the end of 1992, I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, that's all I want to ask. Can we move on, please, then, could you have your diary back again?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've been asked by the Registrar if we can make it 2369.1, just to sort it out from the original page that was exhibited. So that's the diary as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you turn in that to the 22nd of May?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's page 72 of the translation. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] What number do you want to give it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The whole diary, Your Honour. The diary as a whole as opposed to -- because we had one page provisionally exhibited already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Doesn't matter to me, Your Honour but if it's easier for the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Of course.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for His Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry about the microphone. So it will be P2369.1. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Your Honours, page 72 of the translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you have at the same time Exhibit P1830? And 1831 as well? So that we don't -- 1831, please, as well? It's the next document in the binder. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Sir, you recorded in your diary or your notebook the -- a meeting of the executive board at 10.00 and then the Presidency session at 1400, 2.00 p.m., and if you look, please, at the minutes of that meeting, P1830, we can see the actual minutes of the meeting. Looking at it, can you tell us whether you wrote it or whether somebody else kept those minutes?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This part of the copy was poorly scanned, but here I can see a meeting 8.25 and I see that I was the note taker.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, pause. You're on the wrong one, sorry. If you look at the other side of the page, you'll see 22nd --

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the left-hand side, the 22nd May, that is only a plan. And then we come to the operative part. Now, whether it's the 25th of May, I cannot really say because --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the whole diary was scanned and --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you because we have quite a lot to get through today. All I want to do is confirm that on the left-hand side, you have a plan that there was to be a Presidency session at 1400 and if you look, please, at the document for the municipal -- for the minutes, does that show that there was indeed a meeting on the 22nd of May at 1400?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think for the first time we see that the Crisis Staff is now calling itself the Presidency although the people are the same. It was -- was the structure of this group of people the same whether it was called Crisis Staff or War Presidency or War Staff?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the structure was more or less the same, or similar. I have to say that administratively speaking, there was a huge disorder because all sorts of reorganisations were being undertaken and they gave different names to the same services or bodies. At that time, even I wasn't quite sure what was what. So what you are saying now is quite possibly true, probably yes, I would say that by and large they were the same people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. If we look -- if you look at the next document you've been given, which was P1831, I think we can see that they are much the same body because it's headed, "The Crisis Staff of Petrovac municipality" but handwritten at the top is, "War Presidency"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is. At some point in time, the Crisis Staff was renamed as the War Presidency and this is its composition.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Except that later on, they would also incorporate me into it, because of the administrative matters that had to be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, just staying on your diary, as you were starting to tell us, you recorded a meeting with the representatives of the army and as we can see, also, the police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see all the names here but I see Obrad and Jane and they are undoubtedly members of the army and there is something else and then it says Krajina Corps, that is the Drvar one so your conclusion is correct, I guess, although I can't read anything else from this copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. It's a bad copy. In your diary, there are a number of these types of meetings. Was it important, as far as you were concerned, and as far as the other members of the Crisis Staff were concerned, that there should be regular meetings with representatives of the police and the army?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I don't think we need trouble further with -- because it's clear that there was a very lengthy discussion about this. So you can give the two documents back, please, to the usher. I'm sorry, there is perhaps one matter that I ought to deal with on this. Hang on a moment. Yes. I'm sorry, it goes back to what I was asking you further -- earlier. If you look, please, at document P1830, and if you go to the conclusions, under item -- it says item 5 and then conclusion, we can see that the decision that the town should bear the name of Petrovac without the preceding Bosanski was adopted unanimously. So it looks like -- it's my fault for not taking you straight to the document but it looks like that the decision to change the name was taken in 1992. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right, yes. You are right. But the decision to change the name of the town could not be officially taken by this body so that it was adopted officially but it is quite possible that it happened towards the end of 1992 and I mean formally speaking from the legal point of view, this could only be a proposal, that is an initiative, of the municipal administration which had to be confirmed by the republican assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I see so it couldn't be decided at your -- at the municipal level, it had to be decided by the republic level?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it couldn't. This means that this is a definite conclusion. This is an initiative that had been adopted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Can we -- now you can give the document back. I want to move, then, in your diary, please, to the next day, the 23rd, which is our page 76. And we see that there was a session of the Crisis Staff at 1500 hours in the afternoon, and then those -- that list of the members as -- in fact as we see, and then over the other side of the page, on the 24th, the Crisis Staff of ARK, A-R-K, and then duty officer, and then the president and a number, Brdjanin. Now, do you know why you were recording the number -- first of all, are these telephone numbers?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. These are telephone numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And do you know why you were recording in your notebook the number of the duty officer and the number for Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: President Novakovic had given me these numbers for contact in case he was not there and if there is an emergency so that I could establish contact with Crisis Staff. For the same reason the other members, all the other members of the Crisis Staff had their numbers written down here, that is to say the Crisis Staff of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to look, please, at the 24th through some of the documents. It appears it was a very busy day. Could you have, please, first of all --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Your Honour, these were the extra documents which regrettably I left out before. First of all, P1807. I think everybody has had them now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As we'll see, there were three meetings apparently that day and this is the first in time because the number appears to be 13/92.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, they were handed in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. It's okay, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is that right, we can see you were present and the meeting started at 8.25 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's not altogether clear -- well, first, can I remind you just if there is anything which says to you that the document is not authentic or the signature is not authentic, let us know but otherwise, don't bother. Can I ask you to look, please, at the order that was made? It's on page 3 of the translation. The item number 3, the organs of the military police of the police station Petrovac and the military organs of security are hereby ordered to coordinate their work in order to prevent the looting of military public and private property, and then it goes on to talk about the return of looted property. The commander of the service of the public security Petrovac, Gacesa, Captain Trivo Plemic from the base and Captain Nikola Kovacevic from the Petrovac Brigade are hereby charged with the implementation of this task. Upon completing the aforesaid measures they are obliged to inform the Crisis Staff about the measures taken and the results achieved. Can you just tell us who was Captain Plemic?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just remember him in passing. As far as I know, in terms of the surname, he'd have to come from the municipality of Kljuc originally because it is in that municipality that a family with that surname lives and here he is the representative of the military command.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. That's what I wanted to know. All right. And then could you come down to the second item and the decision that was arrived Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. at on that? The executive board shall, brackets, for the third time ask from the companies and organisations to provide plans of production and work during wartime. And so on. Could you have a look now, please, again, at the minutes -- the gazettes that were issued by the regional Crisis Staff, P227? Could you turn to the conclusions for the 13th of May, 1992, which is number 9 in the gazettes? And we see that under conclusion number 1, production in all socially or privately owned companies is to be in line with war plans and we again appeal to the managers of Krajina enterprises to immediately submit their war plans for analysis and approval, and then management posts and enterprises must be filled absolutely by persons loyal to the Serbian republic. Was this decision a response to that conclusion by the autonomous region Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In essence, no. Although formally, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What's the difference?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The difference is in the following: In the previous state, the SFRY, there was an entire set of laws that regulated this particular field, and these laws were taken over later. One of the key regulations in case of war was the obligation to plan and organise wartime production for those companies whose products are indispensable for the survival of the population, for their medical protection and war logistics. In that way, it was simply continued along these lines. Here in this case of the ARK Krajina. As far as this local decision is concerned they actually worked according to the same pattern.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. I think if -- correct me if I'm wrong -- what you're saying is this is what the law said had to happen and the conclusion of the autonomous region and your own decision was merely, effectively, carrying out that law? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Although the AR Krajina was the formal transmission here so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. You can leave that one now. Could you have, please, P1808, which was the next meeting that same day at 1500 hours? There we see, I think, the reference to the problem of the cows, which is under the second agenda item, and you made a long decision about them. And I think -- can I just summarise this? These were really valuable cows because the Court has already seen a lot of discussion about cows but I think as we can see, under the decision that was made on the following page, these cows were eastern Frisian breed bought in Holland and so were considered very valuable; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Dutch will be happy to hear that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm trying to curry favour with the Dutch at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to look please above that. Under the first -- the decision under agenda item 1, the security situation in the municipality, item number 4, in the area of the Petrovac municipality, the disarmament of paramilitary formations and citizens who illegally possess weapons will start on the 24th of May, 1992. So is that right? In Petrovac, the disarming actually started later than apparently it did in other places?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it is so. First of all, I forgot to tell you one thing. The document I looked at a while ago is an authentic document indeed and the remark that the 17th session of the Crisis Staff is also under way is a true one. This is the 18th session. A separate session of the Crisis Staff without the presence of members of military commands. It is possible that later on, in the municipality of Petrovac, this did start, simply for the following reasons because it was done differently in other municipalities. There were armed conflicts there between Serbs and Muslims. There was no such thing in our area. And basically, this disarmament was not disarmament it was arms collection as I explained yesterday. Basically there was no resistance involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And so you needn't tell us if you agree it's authentic. It's only if you're not sure it's authentic you need to tell the Court. All right. Now, you can put that away. Could you have P1809, which is the third meeting that day. The 19th session, held I think that must be 1900 hours, 7.00 in the evening. And --

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we go, please, to the decision under agenda item 2, well, if we look at agenda item 2, the president of the Crisis Staff stated that there are certain functional omissions in his work and the functional organisation of the staff itself should be improved in order to reach and implement the necessary decisions with the highest level of efficiency. If you then go to the decision on the functional improvement, item number 3, "Premises within the building of the public security station Petrovac will be prepared for detaining perpetrators of criminal acts." Then it describes what that means and it includes criminal acts that jeopardise the defensive ability of the Serb people will be detained in a prison until a trial. Prisoners in custody can be utilised for work of a public interest as well as on jobs related to defensive preparations, building of shelters, et cetera. Now, first, what was meant by criminal acts that jeopardised the defensive ability of the Serb people?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Basically, this is a propaganda slogan. All three meetings were held because abruptly, there was no longer any control over the security and safety of citizens and the safety of their property. To give an example, these cows were not important from the point of view of property or the economy as such. The point was that people looted them. They grabbed them. Seized them. So this was a message sent out in very strong terms that this should be stopped, because the looting that started then and also in areas that at that time -- I mean in Muslim villages in the area of Bihac, by the members of our army, this also meant that there was a collapse of the security and safety system for the citizens as such. This ultimately led to the decline of the defensive abilities of the Serb people because people who loot and plunder are not soldiers who are capable of waging a war. That's the point.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you're saying that criminal acts that jeopardise the defensive ability referred to looting?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. Because this became a widespread thing. These people as soldiers plundered and then they went to their homes, they fled to their homes, and this weakened the actual military units.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Then the prisoners in custody can be used for work of public interest and defence preparation. Was that a normal thing that people who had been arrested could be sent out to work on defence, defensive preparations?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, it was customary practice. However, I do remember that if somebody would explicitly refuse to take part in this, there was no way of coercing such a person to do that. I think that's what the chief of police said. However, I must say that a negligible number of people were arrested and only some went through disciplinary proceedings before military organs and they were simply sent to other units that were far away from our area, but this was a very small number.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So if -- sorry, picking up on that, so if people were brought before military courts for acts such as looting, you're saying what would happen to them is they would just be sent to units away from the area?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military court did not function at all. This was a disciplinary decision of their commander or commanding officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: And it was not carried through to the extent that was necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Finally on this document, then we can leave it, at number 8 under the conclusions, there is a decision that the Crisis Staff will analyse implementation of its own decisions in order to determine the responsibility, et cetera, and improve its efficiency. Thank you. You can put that document away now. Can you look now, please, at your diary again, on the 27th of May? And I think there we can see that there is either to be a Crisis Staff meeting at 1400 or there is one, which is to analyse the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. implementation of the decisions by the Crisis Staff, and if you look, please, at P1865, we can see that indeed there was a Crisis Staff meeting on the 27th of May at 1400 hours, and --

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You were present, although in fact your name doesn't appear as attending, I don't think, but we can see under item 2 that you gave a presentation.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: These minutes were taken by the technical secretary. I did not take these notes because as a rule when I would keep the minutes, I would make sure that ultimately when the minutes were completed, they should be signed by the president and this is an omission that is usual when this is being copied. It is true I was present and I see that I also reported on something.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. All right. Can we deal, please, with two of the items that were discussed? Mr. Milanovic informed the meeting on the results of the talks with the representative of the SDA citizens forum. And stated that the representatives, Mr. Hidic and Mr. Ferizovic, spread alarming rumours by saying that the Muslim citizens want to emigrate collectively. And then Mr. Ivanic said that the citizens forum said that the Muslims were loyal citizens and accused Safet Hidic and Mustafa Ferizovic of illegal arming. Can we put it this way. Not to spend too long on it. Does it appear there was a split between the SDA, between those who wanted to -- wanted everybody to emigrate and those who said they should remain in Petrovac and support the government?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say that there was a split, as far as the SDA is concerned. However, in that period, the Muslims as a community were in a precarious position because of all these circumstances that have been documented. There was a forum of citizens as a more or less non-political body, which included prominent figures from the authorities and from political echelons in general. They mediated in order to reduce tensions, and in order to have the Muslims protected, and in order to have their interests protected as much as possible. It is true that this was discussed in such a way. However, I wish to point out the following: Ivanic also presented the convictions of some citizens that he had contacted and of course he had contact only with a few people, and since he was a Serb, probably they were telling him what he wanted to hear. You know how people act when they are worried about the safety of their property and things like that. That's the position that they are in then. At any rate everybody was saying what they were convinced of.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Yes, thank you. And then you, as you noted in your own diary, informed the Crisis Staff on the implementation of the decisions in respect of the previous session of the Crisis Staff. Now, finally could you turn to the conclusion? The last one, a memorandum is to be sent to the Krnjeusa local commune informing them that the Crisis Staff they have formed is illegal. Could you have a look again, please, at the gazettes of the regional Crisis Staff, Exhibit P227? And could you go to the conclusions for the 9th of May, number 6? We see there that decisions adopted by the war staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina are to be strictly respected and item number 3 no Crisis Staff can be formed in any enterprise. Now, was that anything to do with the decision that there was an illegal Crisis Staff in Krnjeusa?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Krnjeusa the Crisis Staff was illegal because they tried to establish a Crisis Staff and to make it impossible to seize looted property. Armoured vehicles were used to take it away. They were very persistent in safeguarding their right to looting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Who -- was this a Serb-inhabited commune?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. All right. Thank you. You can put that document away, then. If we move very quickly then through the end of May in your diary, on the 28th of the 5th, you noted that there was -- you had to organise a meeting between the Crisis Staff and the brigade command staff but that you would not be there.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's not that I couldn't attend. It was a note that I was to give the president, after consultations with the brigade command, it is they who said they could not attend but in point of fact they simply did not want to attend the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And why was that?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, the Crisis Staff kept telling them that they were responsible for the large-scale plunder and disorder and all the rest, and their representatives did not like that at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Sorry, just a -- all right. Can we move, then, please to now the 1st of June in your diary? And that's at our page 82. You do a list of the presidents of the local communes and then if you go to the part where you list the 23rd session of the Crisis Staff at 1615, that's our page 84, Your Honour. Again you're analysing the implementation of the Crisis Staff decisions from the previous session and then a decision to send a report to an authorised command in the territory of the municipality regarding the municipal request to coordinate the security activities, provided that all factors are involved in the plan, TO, police and army, and then was it you who was to do the memorandum?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a rule, I wrote those. I can't remember this concrete one but yes, as a rule, the president asked me to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Why was there to be a report sent to the authorised command? What was the problem? I mean, why were you having a request to coordinate all the security activities?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you the reason, because mostly the disorder and the disarray, were mostly caused by their members, yes, you're right but there were also other problems. There would be shots fired in the town, there was violence, and those men wore uniforms and the civilian police couldn't even arrest them. The civilian police could only perhaps take down their names but then would have to let them go.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, now I'm afraid I did miss one more document from the end of May. Could you have a look at Exhibit P211? This is a -- apparently a telegram, this one in particular, I think, comes from Sanski Most. I mean this particular copy. Dated the 28th of May, sent by the Autonomous Region of Krajina Crisis Staff and some conclusions, and could you look at item number 7? That states if Muslims and Croats or members of the SDA Party of Democratic Action wish to leave or move out of the Autonomous Region of Krajina they must enable the endangered Serbian people against whom unprecedented genocide is being conducted to move collectively into their places, i.e. they must facilitate an exchange based on reciprocity. And that, in fact, we can see if we look at the meeting, the gazette, for the 28th, for the 29th of May, in fact, which is number 23 in the gazette, something that had been decided and I think there is an earlier one as well but I lost my note on that. Yeah. Now, if you just look at that and then could you have, please, P1869?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: While the witness has -- looks at the document, Ms. Korner, if perhaps at some point in time before this witness goes home, if you could provide us with a list of which of the documents that he has been referred to and acknowledged directly or indirectly as authentic, come from AID?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I will, certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you see there that Mr. Latinovic under the agenda -- first of all the agenda, 1, discussing the conclusions of the autonomous region Krajina Crisis Staff in Banja Luka, Mr. Latinovic reads the conclusion of the AR Crisis Staff in Banja Luka reached at the session on the 29th of May, 1992. Now, pausing there, would that mean that the person who had been to the meeting of the Crisis Staff would read the conclusion?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would, yes, unless it has arrived in a written form.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. This is what I wanted -- because we'll see that the first Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. thing that you adopted was that all Muslims and Croats who so wish be enable to evacuate from the territory of the ARK, et cetera which is almost identical wording to what we see in this telegram. Now, I know it's difficult. Can you remember whether this particular instruction which you followed came by telegram or whether somebody had personally attended the meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember how these conclusions reached us. Possibly they were faxed but I'd say it was most likely that it was to the signals unit that they reached but perhaps there was a messenger who brought them. I don't remember it, because of all the security measures around the Banja Luka airport, which looked rather curious to me so that -- but be that as it may, these decisions were adopted and they are as they are. And the principle of reciprocity in such a law after the war was established and it was only the high commissioner who vacated that law and it was a law on the manner of using the abandoned property but I mean, no, the law was unenforceable any way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You've said a number of things. First of all, you said the high commissioner reversed it. In other words, people were entitled to have back their property in the areas which they had left, is that what you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But this in fact -- well, the effect was, wasn't it, to create or to try and create an ethnically pure area?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot talk about somebody's intentions but, yes, what happened would allow such a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Anyhow, can you just tell us, while we are on this topic, who would normally attend the meetings of the regional Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was President Novakovic who was supposed to attend those meetings ex officio. If he was prevented then I think it was Dragan Milanovic, who was a member of parliament, perhaps he was also to go there ex officio, but I didn't communicate with him much because we did not particularly like each other, I have to say. So that Mr. Bogdan Latinovic, who was the president of the executive board, would be there instead of him, so that when President Novakovic couldn't Latinovic went, but it was usually one of those front men --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- who went to those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. You can put that document away now. I'm sorry, trying to keep track of so many different documents. I need you to go back in your diary just one moment to the 26th of May, our page 78. You wrote down at the bottom of that entry for the 26th of May, three names. Can you just very briefly tell us who these people were?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are individuals who were plundering the Muslim population as an organised group and were involved also in other violent acts, as was established by the police, and there was somebody else I can't remember his name because I didn't know it at the time, I was to brief the public Prosecutor about this so that he could prepare the indictment and so that everything could be prepared for their arrest.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. You said apart from plundering, they were involved in other violent acts. What were they?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I heard, they were involved in so-called racketeering. That is they went to some households, that they thought there could be some money and would threaten that they would kill a member of the family unless all the money was given to them. And I know that once they abducted a minor, I think it was a 14 or 15 year old girl I'm not quite sure but I saw her father crying. It was a Muslim ethnicity. I mean both father and the daughter were Muslim, and I know that the police organised a pursuit to find the abducted girl.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. Thank you. I'm sorry I had to go back there. I'd like to go on moving, please, through June. Could you look, please, at your entry for the 2nd of June in your diary? You've got an entry, check the situation about the payments of pensions in the territory of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. Very briefly, whose pensions?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pensioners. When AR Krajina was proclaimed it was to adopt all the duties of a government. I mean to adopt all the duties of the republic, and the government of Krajina was to assume all the roles, all the duties, of a republican government, that is payments, then different funds and how they are to be funded, how they are to be replenished and that includes the pensions fund so I was asked to see whether this was in working order because I suppose there were some delays in payments.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And then that same day, if you go to the next part, page, of your diary, this is our page 87, there is reference to the meeting about the incident in Biscani. What had happened in Biscani that required a meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I suppose there was some violent act which had to do with the security of the Muslim population because Biscani is largely inhabited by Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you remember now --

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly -- possibly it was the -- this incident that I mentioned when the girl was abducted. I cannot really pinpoint it, but I can't think of anything else. I can't think what else could it have been.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I just want to show you, please, one short new document which you saw in the interview. That's disclosure 2.233 which will become P2451. It's actually dated the 27th of May. And it asks the military post to issue two automatic rifles and two hand grenades to arm the driver of the municipal Crisis Staff and the cryptographic data protection operator. Can you just tell us why it was necessary to arm these two people like that?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The driver of the municipal -- of the official vehicle of the municipal hall often took the president through areas where there was combat going on. The president really took risks and that is how he got killed eventually and that is why it was thought necessary to issue the driver with an automatic rifle. As for the signals centre and the -- they had a so-called crypto room and the only person who was involved with codes was admitted into that room. During the war, they were all armed -- before that, before that, they had pistols but when the war started, this was stepped up and they were issued with automatic rifles. Because that kind of work was considered very important and very confidential.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Okay. Thank you. Now can we move, please, on again to further in your diary, no. In fact, I think you need to look, please, now at P1870, which is the 4th of June. First of all, the first agenda item, the president, Mr. Novakovic informed those in attendance about the talks that he had with Dr. Karadzic and General Mladic. That goes back, does it, to what you told us yesterday, that Mr. Novakovic had access to the two leaders?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And were you present when he met with them?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, not then. He went to those meetings alone, and there was no need for me to go with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, the second item is the incident in Biscani, so that's come up again and if you look at agenda item 2 --

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've had a look, and it all came back to me. I think I really know what this is about. It's that -- at that time a whole Muslim family was slain, was killed. I cannot remember their last name because I was a newcomer there, but I know that the first name of the man was Sevko, and in one night, he, his wife, a daughter and a son, who were quite young, in their late teens or maybe 20 year old, were all killed, and the police investigated the case, there were different ideas, various guesses and hypotheses were made as to who could have been the perpetrators but that is what this is about, the killing of that family.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. You can put that document away now. And can we move, please, in your diary to the 7th of June? That's page 92. Now, there you record, it's headed meeting in Palanka. Is that a meeting that you attended? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a meeting which I should have attended and perhaps I did, because on a couple of occasions I did go to meetings in Palanka, once it was in winter time and once it was in summertime. So this could have been that meeting that took place that summer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I'd now like to you have a look, please, at P229. This is a document headed, "Sanski Most, 7th of June, 1992. Conclusions adopted at a subregional meeting of the political representatives of the municipalities of" and it includes Bosanski Petrovac. It was sent to the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Banja Luka and the leadership and the 1st Krajina Corps. Conclusion number 1: It is necessary to declare a state of war in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and -- because of the situation in the municipalities, and it goes on, Ustasha troops are preparing to immediately attack the Autonomous Region of Krajina. If you look, please, at your notebook, the problem of refugees and prisoners, and then you say state of war to be proclaimed. Now, does that seem to suggest that it was this meeting that you were attending?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Palanka -- Lusci Palanka is in the municipality of Sanski Most, is it not?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I'm not -- I don't think you've had a chance to read through this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So Your Honour, it may be appropriate because it's a lengthy document if we break now and the witness has a chance to take the document with him and just read it over the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a 25 minute break now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Your Honour, before Ms. Korner starts may I address the Court about Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Do you want to wait for your client?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Otherwise we'll have a speech. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Your Honour, I spoke with Mr. Ackerman over the break and with the Court's leave he would be here at 1.30. I think that would be the best but of course if you disagree he'll be here sooner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. It's okay with me. It's okay with me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Judge, you've had a look at that, I think, document now, over the break, does that remind you about the meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I do recall the meeting now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I ask first of all, do you remember the names of the people who attended from the other municipalities? We see in your notebook that Stakic is written down there. Was he the person who attended from Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that he was, and I probably wrote his number down in order to keep it up to date because numbers changed very often so I used this opportunity to have the exact telephone number because I needed exact telephone numbers in order to be able to contact people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Sanski Most, did you know Rasula?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you remember if he was there?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly who the persons present were but as a rule the presidents were present and perhaps if they were unable to attend, then they would send a representative and that is the capacity in which I went.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Pasic from Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. We see that you made a note that in your diary of Basara and he apparently -- the note you put then is the RSK assets to be put at the disposal of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. Does that mean that he was at this meeting as well?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly he was, or he made this proposal, or this has to do with some material resources or weapons, I don't know exactly. These are resources from the Republika Srpska Krajina that were given to the Autonomous Region of Krajina for their use. At this meeting I probably did not take part in the debate. I was there only to collect information and to convey information and that is why I did not take a lot of notes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. If we just briefly summarise what was being said there, they wanted -- the first conclusion to declare a state of war so that war tribunals could start functioning. The second dealing with the corridor. Then the third dealing with the reorganisation of the former JNA, which was by then the VRS. Four, a demand that General Talic purge the 1st Krajina Corps of Muslims and Croats. Five, that the borders of the Autonomous Region of Krajina were defined. And then six, all seven municipalities in our subregion agree that Muslims and Croats should move out of our municipalities until a level is reached where Serbian authority can be maintained, request the Crisis Staff of the autonomous region provide a corridor. And if the leadership fails to solve this issue, our seven municipalities will take all Muslims and Croats under military escort from our municipalities. Now, I want to know, sir, you were really, as you say, taking notes so you could brief your own municipality. Was Mr. Novakovic there with you?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I wouldn't have been present had he been there. I believe that he sent me there purely out of courtesy towards the others, since they had invited him. I believe that he thought that this meeting was not all that important and that's why he sent me as an envoy. Had it been important, I would have taken a lot of notes, and I probably would have had a great deal of the content involved in my notes. As a matter of fact, I don't even remember that such conclusions were reached. I think that they actually wrote it this way subsequently and in an arbitrary fashion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can I ask you this? It says all seven municipalities agreed to these conclusions. Were you in a position to agree that on behalf of your president?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have any authority in this regard and that is upon which I base my assertion that this was written off the cuff and later. Muslims were not an impediment to the organisation of government in our municipality so we certainly would not have voted in favour of such a conclusion because it would have been pointless. Secondly, there are differing decisions involved here and also there are certain conditions that are put forth that are wrong, that are inexpedient and so on. Last but not least, may I note that the actual language, the lexicon of this text, is troublesome.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean that it is legally unfounded. Quite simply, it is illiterate from an administrative point of view. There is a lot of contradictory elements involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. The threat to take all Muslims and Croats under military escort from our municipalities to the centre of Banja Luka, do you recall something like that being said at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This meeting -- since I do not remember it -- was some kind of informal chat, and it certainly was not binding in any way, because had such important decisions actually been taken, I would have recorded them verbatim in my notebook.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Whatever conclusions were adopted by these political representatives, as it's stated, in your view, was that going to be binding on any one of the seven?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This could not have been binding. I think that this was done in one of the municipalities. At the end of the meeting it was probably Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. agreed informally that somebody should draft this document and send it to the relevant authorities. So basically, whoever wrote this did this on his own. I don't know who did it exactly. I see with fraternal greetings written here but there is not a full copy of the page so I can't see who signed it. Basically this was sent on behalf of the party.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. In fact the only -- as you say, the only conclusion that you seem to have noted down is that a state of war should be proclaimed, which was in the first conclusion. However, I want you to look now, please, if you would, at -- just a moment, so I get my note right --

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Is there something else you want to say about this?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a discussion on the proclamation of a state of war and also the problem of population resettlement because it says here the problem of refugees. That's what it says in my notebook so all of this was discussed but conclusions were not formally adopted. Somebody wrote them subsequently, later. Had they been adopted at the actual meeting, they would not have been worded as they are now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I think you need to look, before you go on, at document P1873, which was the 28th session of the Crisis Staff on the 9th of June and if you go, please, to the conclusion and under item 2, you will see Mr. Latinovic informed the participants about the conclusions adopted at the meeting, that was held at Lusci Palanka with the representatives of the seven municipalities. Now, did you inform Mr. Latinovic or do you think that Mr. Latinovic may have been there, or alternatively did he get the conclusions or can't you say?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that Mr. Latinovic was at the meeting then but it was not our meeting. I meant the municipal level. So that's why I did not take a lot of notes. Possibly I accompanied Mr. Latinovic or perhaps I only noted the meeting in Palanka in view of the questions that should be discussed and perhaps Latinovic was at the meeting then. I cannot say exactly. It's been a long time now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I appreciate that but he was actually informing them about the conclusions. I should ask you this: Had you ever seen those written conclusions before you looked at them today?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember having seen them earlier, but their content is such that it does correspond to what was going on at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not Mr. Latinovic held the views that the Muslims and Croats should be removed from the municipality of Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not hold such a view. I know that because at one point in time, after the civic forum which we already mentioned gave a proposal on the part of the Muslims that they should join the army too, but that they should not go to those front lines where Serbs and Muslims clashed directly, but also they asked that the commander of that unit should be a Serb. So that possible responsibility for losing a position would not fall on them. I mean so that no one would suspect them of having done anything. Mr. Latinovic himself agreed to become commander of that unit. He was a reserve officer of the former JNA so he had the professional skills involved and he asked me whether I wanted to be assistant for information in that unit. So that is how I know that he was against this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then we see above, before we get to conclusion, there is a long discussion about the Petrovac medical centre and we see that it's stated that the government of the Serbian region Krajina Banja Luka is the organisational organ and it will certainly determine in its decisions what will be financed by funds. Was this in relation to funds required for the purchase of essential medical supplies, as we can see?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. You can put that away. And could you have a look now, please, at P236, which is the next meeting of the Crisis Staff for that same day -- I'm sorry, it's the following day, I beg your pardon. And there we see that the agenda proposed by Mr. Novakovic as the president was first that conclusions adopted by the Autonomous Region of Krajina Crisis Staff. Under item 1 the president of the Crisis Staff briefed those present on the conclusions adopted by the AR Krajina Crisis Staff in Banja Luka and then this: Subregions of the municipalities forwarded certain proposals to the AR Krajina government for a prompt organisation of the army and regulations of essential services in order to facilitate government functions and relations between the Krajina government and the municipalities on its territory. Now, we don't see anything further was said about that. Do you recall that discussion? Because you were apparently there.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there. The technical secretary took notes. I cannot remember individually what various participants in the discussions said but the topics discussed at this meeting, on the 10th of June, were brought up on a variety of occasions later as well, so what is obvious is that it was discussed at this meeting and not only at this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. All that I want to know is whether you're able to tell us whether this bit about the subregions forwarding certain proposals relates back to those conclusions of the 7th of June? If you can't remember, say so straight away.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this conclusion was aimed at that, to ask the AR Krajina to function in the way in which it had been proclaimed, that is to say to establish functional organs of authority and government, because definitely they had proclaimed themselves as such but they barely functioned if at all in certain areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And which areas were those?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The area of the economy. They hardly functioned there at all. In the area of health care, not the basic prerequisites were there, in terms of financing health care and so on. Also, in the area of schooling. Pension and health funds were not being replenished properly. Salaries were hardly ever paid. Quite simply there was a societal collapse. The state of war had already started and such things considered of -- were considered to be of vital jeopardy in terms of everything that was going on. When you ask me about those conclusions, the answer is no, because we can see from these minutes that for us, population resettlement was not an issue at all. It was not topical at all. Because of the actual numbers involved, and the actual relations involved, we never thought that we were jeopardised in any way by the Muslims. At least not those from the area of our municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. On that topic, this is something you talked about in the interview at page 74, by the 9th of June, were people, Muslims, non-Serbs, wanting to leave the municipality?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that they wanted this but because of everything that happened, and it's my understanding that safety was under control so to speak or had safety been under control and if there weren't such incidents like the one in Biscani and some others, they would not have asked to be resettled.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they asked for it only because they felt threatened.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you have a look, I think you refer to this in your own diary, if you look at page -- our page 93, for the 9th of June, your entry, it's on the opposite side where you talk about vacations. At the bottom of the page, that page, you talk about departure of citizens from Petrovac, under -- sorry, questions to be raised with the Crisis Staff, departure of citizens from Petrovac. So was this becoming a problem?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the 9th of June?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: M'hm.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This could have been or rather it most probably had to do with the departure of Muslims from Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. All right, so it was starting, at the very least?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. Perhaps even earlier, people who had the opportunity to leave Petrovac did leave it earlier, on an individual basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then can we look, please, at the conclusions --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour we will come to that. I don't know why you're being handed it at this stage. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I agree, Ms. Korner. It misled me completely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think if the Registry waits until we get to it and then we will hand it in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Conclusions, please, under item 2, this is -- sorry, the conclusions under item 3, the military command must apply to the civilian authorities for any mobilisation of people, material goods or equipment. In other words -- does that mean if they wanted to -- if the military command wanted more people, goods or equipment, they had to apply to the Crisis Staff or the assembly if it was sitting?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is on my page number 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. It's under item 3, I'm sorry, in -- I'm sorry, this is back to the -- I'm so sorry, the minutes of the meeting I want to go back to, not your diary, under Exhibit P236, under the item 3, where the -- Mr. Brankovic?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have found it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your conclusion is correct. Formally, the military command was supposed to address the National Defence department, that is a civilian authority. However, they carried out arbitrary mobilisation of personnel, notably material resources. For example, they would mobilise all the cars that they liked. They just get the driver out, take his papers for the car from him, and they would just take the car. This was not real mobilisation. It was basically theft. Later on, according to the law, the state was supposed to pay for these vehicles if they were damaged or lost. That is why there was a conflict between the civilian authorities and the military command. That is one of the reasons for these clashes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then, under 2, I want to ask you about, the Petrovac municipal staff remains in its full composition but it will be resubordinated to the military command until a written decision or decree regulating its status is issued by the government of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. What was that about?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was about the Territorial Defence staff. Its status was not regulated legally in that transition period. That is the staff that was headed by Mr. Vrzina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. I think that's all we need, thank you very much, on that document. Now, can we just move through -- yes. Could we move, please, to the 13th of June, in your diary, please? Page -- I'm sorry, Your Honours, page 100. And at the same time, could you be handed, please, P1876? Now, you record the meeting of the 33rd session of the Crisis Staff and we can see that, although I think there is an error, maybe it's in our translation. Yes, it is, Your Honour. It's been -- in the translation, it's clear from the original it's the 13th of June, under minutes as well although it's been translated as 16th of June. I don't think that matters. Now, the agenda, again, this time I think it's clear you were actually taking the notes as well?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the note taker and I think that this is the 13th of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. When you were taking the notes, was that notes that you kept in your diary which you then expanded on or were you taking, which you then typed up, or did you actually write them out by hand at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was note taker, then I would as a rule write things down in my own notebook or perhaps sometimes on a piece of paper. That is where I would actually write the draft, to act as a reminder later, and then as soon as the meeting would end, then I would dictate the minutes to a typist and then I would take it to the president for him to take a look, and if everything was all right, then he would sign the minutes. That is why as a rule all of my minutes were signed because they had been verified and at the following meeting, whenever I would be the -- whenever I was the note taker at the previous meeting and this is not included in the minutes then it would be submitted to the Crisis Staff for verification.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Okay. If we move fairly quickly through this, the agenda item number 1 a decision on how to accommodate the -- I think it's a military post, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then under that, we see if we look to the decision, you will see that after that -- I'm sorry, item number 2 was a report on the security situation. In the discussion that followed, it was stated that there was some negligence which however did not seriously affect the security station. Disarmament of the paramilitary formations and citizens who are in illegal possession of arms is to be continued and brought to a close. And I think you've already explained who was being disarmed. But then this. After that, they unanimously reached the following: The bodies in charge are to finalise activities regarding the disarmament of paramilitary formations and citizens who illegally possess weapons, appropriate repressive measures are to be taken against individuals who took part in the illegal armament of the paramilitary organisation and citizens. What was that referring to? Or who? Who were the people who had been illegally arming what you've already told us effectively was the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in essence, I myself never had any knowledge in terms of who it could have been. There were rumours that they were their leaders, as Mr. Ivanic mentioned on that day, or somebody else perhaps, I can't remember exactly. However, there were rumours that this was done by some Serbs who had smuggled weapons. This other rumour is something I know a bit more about, namely once a security colonel came to see the president and he warned about that, that some Serbs were bringing in weapons and selling them to Muslims but I never found out, nor did anybody else ever find out officially or could have anybody found out, about who had done this. Especially as far as the Muslims are concerned. In my presence, not a single name was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Then can we move, please, to the next decision under 5, where we see that the representatives requested a postal service, that's the representatives, I think, of the military post, to make it impossible for the enemy to wire tap conversations. They also requested the connection of the Petrovac post office to the Banja Luka postal service and to implement the Autonomous Region of Krajina Crisis Staff decisions concerning the removal of the executive staff of non-Serb ethnicity. Before we look at those decisions, are you saying -- was this the military saying you, the Crisis Staff, should carry out the instructions of the Autonomous Region of Krajina Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, yes. It was the army which requested it. Well, they -- the army had lots of requests and demands put to us. They kept bringing pressure on us to have the director of the post office removed, dismissed, because he was a Muslim. But he did his work well so there was no reason.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. In fact it looks like this was -- it doesn't actually make that clear -- okay, if we very quickly, the decisions that dealt with that, we can see, perhaps Your Honour we needn't look at them again. They were on the 11th of May, the 13th of May, and the 26th of May. Were you aware of those decisions by the regional Crisis Staff? Don't worry about -- well, first of all, were you aware of these?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff decision concerning what? The autonomous region? I'm sorry I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm trying to do this too quickly. Could you have the gazettes again, please? 227. Can you look at the conclusions for the 11th of May, which are number 7 in the gazette? Management posts in the Krajina enterprises must be filled by persons who are absolutely loyal to the Serbian republic. You see that? That's under number 5.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see it but I did see it somewhere today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. If you look at -- I'm sorry, it's a bit of a mess, I know.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we got the pages and the documents mixed up. Yes. The pages are not in the right order. But yes, I was familiar with the contents of that decision, that there was such a decision and I suppose that the army command is requesting it in this relation. We resisted it for a very long time but eventually this man was dismissed and I met him after that and he was very cut up about the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In fact, dismissals of non-Serbs were taking place, weren't they, in Petrovac? Whatever you personally felt about it.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were taking place.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And I don't think we need anything else on that meeting. Thank you very much. Can we look, please, then, at the meeting for the next day, the 14th of June, which is Exhibit P245?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 245, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Previously, Ms. Korner, I mean just to make sure that I am not mistaken but previously you had referred to the -- the witness to the meetings of the 11th May, the 13th of May and the 26th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I didn't take him through them but Your Honours can see them in the gazettes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So now we are moving to a different topic?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I just wanted to make sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You're absolutely right. We are now back to the Petrovac meetings, not the regional meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is all on the same topic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Again, I think you took the minutes for this one, didn't you, Mr. Radojko, judge?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is an AID document, in passing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Item number 1, Mr. Novakovic opens the discussion and pointed out that it was necessary to adopt positions at the level of the Autonomous Region of Krajina on how to deal with inhabitants who are not loyal to the Serbian republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This meeting was quite a late meeting. It looks like 20 past 10.00 in the evening. That day, there was another meeting of these municipalities, and this time in Korcanica, I think, on the 14th of June. Do you know if Mr. Novakovic had attended a meeting that day?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. He perhaps told us, but because of the sequence of those meetings, it's quite possible that he went to Korcanica and therefore conveyed these meeting for a later time, for a later hour so that he could come back.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Just to look at -- I don't think this time you did attend the meeting. Yes, I'm sorry, the meeting in Korcanica. Okay. Now, then, we see that Mr. Vrzina reported on the situation in the municipality and conveyed the brigade command's request that Muslims be excluded from the work of the municipal assembly administrative organs and that arrested persons suspected on reasonable grounds of participating in undermining the Serbian republic defence or preparing an attack on its institutions and citizens should not be released from detention before trial. And then requested that Muslim inhabitants who had pledged loyalty to the Serbian republic be included in defence preparations. So again, the military was reinforcing what it had said the previous day, about Muslims effectively being excluded and indeed -- well, excluded. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is right. The army never stopped putting pressure. They had learned that there was an intention to form a unit made of Muslims and incorporated in the defence and they opposed it. And also when he talks about these detainees, Mr. Gacesa, who was the chief of police said and I don't think you can find it in the minutes, told the president that the police practically had no evidence against the majority of those detainees and that they would have to release them, and of course, the members of the military command learned about that and they spread this information around the units on the front and therefore the pressure not to release them, so this conclusion is not based on law but it is a factual conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. You can put that away and I'm going to just ask you to look at the record of the meeting of the, as it's now called Sansko-Unska area which is P247, just to ask you about one aspect of what was said. I think it's a proposal, if we look at the page in our copy it begins 00471394, joint positions, I think it must be to be taken, at the 15th of June session in Banja Luka. Because the date of this document is the 12th -- the 14th of June at 1200 hours. We think the work of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina under wartime circumstances should be much more serious, that its politicians and experts should pay much more attention to the problems in all constituent municipalities of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. Very much, sir, what you've expressed to us today, that you didn't think it was working properly. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is, yes. You're quite right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then there is a next suggestion, we propose that Vojo Kupresanin be appointed president of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina given the position he currently occupies as president of the assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. Now, Mr. Brdjanin, were you aware, had been the vice-president of the assembly? Did you know from anything that was said to you by Mr. Novakovic why Mr. Brdjanin had become the president of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Novakovic never talked about it, so one knew or didn't know such things, and I knew about Mr. Kupresanin more than about Mr. Brdjanin from the media rather, Brdjanin would turn up as a signatory or something but believe me, I never even looked what office he indicated on whose behalf he was signing it. But when decisions are made you just don't look up those things.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What was the view that was held by Mr. Novakovic or you yourself, perhaps we ought to split this. It's a double question. Do you know what views Mr. Novakovic held about Mr. Brdjanin at all?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Novakovic and as far as the officials are concerned, Brdjanin, Kupresanin, others, my opinions were usually based on the opinions of Mr. Novakovic, Mr. Milanovic, who was a MP, and other people who communicated with them. My impression was that they didn't think particularly favourably of Mr. Brdjanin, that is they did not think he was up to the task and they mostly recounted various anecdotes and jokes about him. Mr. Novakovic was a true leader and on various occasions I heard him talk with Mr. Karadzic and other people from the top-most ranks of the Serb leadership so that he did not depend on Mr. Brdjanin. He was not subordinated to him in any way or anybody else in Banja Luka.
