But it was thought generally that the Banja Luka SDS leadership was not good and they were frequently changed and a couple of those SDS presidents in Banja Luka were prone to alcohol so -- and these are commonly known facts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now you say that he wasn't -- Mr. Novakovic wasn't personally subordinated to him in any way or anyone else in Banja Luka. But as we have been going through all these decisions of the Crisis Staff in Petrovac, the decisions made by the regional Crisis Staff, what sort of impact were they having? I mean you refer to them quite a lot.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just mentioned what kind of personal relations there were. But I did not -- they did not affect decisively the functioning of the administration and Mr. Novakovic personally urged everybody to respect the decisions regardless of the persons behind them, whether it has to do with the military or the Krajina, that is AR Krajina or the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is if one thought that the decisions were purposeful they were put through. Only the decisions which made no sense, which served no purpose, and did not have anything to do with our area, they were not implemented or could not be, especially those which were quite illegal and could therefore entail very grave consequences at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you say decisions which made no sense, served no purpose. In other words they weren't applicable to the conditions in your area?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Excuse me, Judge I am going object to the leading question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I thought we had made that clear but I will rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please rephrase the question because you are suggesting to the witness as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I thought we had already been through it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What do you mean by decisions which made no sense and served no purpose and did not have anything to do with our area?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally warned Mr. Novakovic against a number of such decisions, decisions which were unenforceable, one of such was to carry out complete mobilisation, and the mobilisation had been done and over with a long time ago and it came from a source which was simply not acceptable. Decisions which will not mean any movement forward or do not serve any purpose. It is illegal to dismiss persons who are allegedly disloyal. First, you cannot arbitrarily decide who is loyal and who isn't. I remember, for instance, an event when we were expected to dismiss our clerks, our personnel, and I told President Novakovic, I believe that Latinovic was present, that that would be a very dangerous decision because at the end of the war, when it was all over, and when the -- an end was put to the chaos, the municipality will need ten times its normal budget to pay compensation to all these people. That will have to recognise them, that will have to compensate for all the pain and everything that they had suffered through it all so that in relation to this decision, we told people to just wait, that is we froze their jobs, we did not dismiss them, and that was the suggestion that we gave to other companies to act on their own discretion, their own discretion, we simply did not want to assume the responsibility for anything like it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But you did in fact, I thought we had already dealt with this, you did in fact dismiss people, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, formally, they were not dismissed, but actually they did stop working, but we provided the basis, we provided the grounds so that after it was all over, they could get their jobs back again and so that seniority, years of service, could again be included, could be added, because these people were qualified people and we cared about the services, about the service that they could render.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So you didn't approve of the decision, you thought in your view that it was illegal, and you tried to get round it but did you actually implement it?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I told you, it was implemented.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's a long way around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a long way around but basically my mind is still working on this. What would have been the consequences or consequence or consequences had the Crisis Staff of Bosanski Petrovac not implemented that decision, had they kept all those employees in their employment? What would you have expected to happen? Or what was the feeling at the time if those decisions were not implemented?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there is no doubt that we would have been removed from the places which we held. There were two mechanisms that they used to bring pressure. One was informal, through people, through the population, and they would simply -- they would apply various methods to start hounding us, to start protesting against what we did, on various occasions armed men broke into our offices and there was also a different pressure constantly brought through the army, and you can see it from the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. It's okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And we just tried to weigh the two and see which evil would be a lesser evil.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, can we please --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour -- I'm sorry, I'll start again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry, Ms. Korner. I interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no, no. It's quite all right. I was going to move on anyhow. If Mr. Cunningham doesn't object I would like to lead because it's the quickest way of doing it about these different signatures on these documents that we looked at on the 16th of June. It's in the interview at page 76 is there any real dispute about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I don't have any problems leading on this topic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Could you have, please -- you can take that document back again, and you need to have now, please, P183 -- no, I'm sorry, yes, 1833, and then 1877.1 and 1877.2? Before we look at the contents, you looked at these I think in the interview, judge, and you were able to explain why they had different signatures.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You want me to explain that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm just going to put it to you, if you -- as briefly as I can, and if you can just tell me if you still adhere to your answer: That the technical service would produce various copies of the minutes that on this occasion were taken, and would then seek the signatures of the people who attended the meeting, but if she couldn't reach them all at the same time before copies were sent away, each would sign the available copy. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I think you took the view when you looked at them that probably the original version is the one that we have as our Exhibit P1833. Which has got written in the top, "Crisis Staff, 57/92." And the word in the original.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. But basically, they are all originals except that the signatures are not, but in terms of the contents, they are all that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And I think you also told us that after the meetings, the notes would be transformed into the typed set of minutes, some would be filed in the archives, and others would be used, as you put it, for operational matters, in other words were they sent to the people who needed them?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in principle, somebody would come to the municipal hall, they would be given it personally and that is why you don't have signatures everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: And those which were accessible to a clerk, they would immediately sign it, so you can see that Novakovic signed here so it means that he was simply available.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. If you just hold on, then, to P1833, the original ones, and give the other ones back and I want to ask you about the contents. I think you recorded this meeting in your own notes, if you look at your diary for the 16th of June and it's our page 106.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. If we look at the agenda, discussion on the situation, the problem of the Muslims and the army, the military pressure is still carrying on, and then Mr. Gacesa talked about a list of some 40 people or so considered to be organised as a separate group or to have acted from fundamentalist Islamic positions. The operation to disarm Muslim paramilitary units and citizens is continued so at that stage it was made absolutely clear, was it, in the Crisis Staff meeting that paramilitary units and citizens were Muslims? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Most of the persons included in the above-mentioned list have been found to possess illegal weapons. There are two possible options, one that a certain number of persons who could be a potential threat be isolated but not on the premises of the SJB, and the other that extremists be isolated outside Petrovac. The discussion continued and the view prevailed that the isolation of extremists outside Petrovac would be dangerous to themselves and that it was best to isolate them in a well guarded facility on the outskirts of town and then decision: All individuals who possess illegal weapons or have been registered as Muslim extremists thus posing a potential threat shall be detained and held in custody. Now, what was this register of Muslim extremists?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Officially, such a register could not be established. To the best of my knowledge this was done on the basis of initial operative knowledge obtained by the police themselves. Some people did indeed have weapons that were found, as far as I know, and other people were put on this list according to their own arbitrary assessments. You see, when they say here the 13 are inaccessible, these are people who had already left the territory of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I'd like you to have a look, please, at P1840. It's jumping forward a little bit in time. Lists for persons for whom Bosanski Petrovac public security station has ordered isolation and I think you saw this during the interview. All Muslims; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then they say that 29 people were taken to do labour at Kozila but we'll come on to Kozila in a moment, on the 1st of July, did you know any of them personally?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew a man here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which one is that?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm looking at the rest of the names to see whether I knew anybody else. I knew one for sure, or actually I knew two. One was Midhat Druzic nicknamed Midho. I knew him by sight. I know him when I read the nickname too. But I knew Fuad Ferizovic better the one nicknamed Beli, because he's a lawyer too. So we had professional contacts as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Would you have described him as a Muslim extremist? First of all him, first of all, number 9, Midhat Druzic, would you have described him as a Muslim extremist?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, I did not really contact him. I just heard about him. I heard that he was expressing some extremist views. In essence this was a man with hardly any education and in my assessment a person with a modest IQ. At one point, apparently he said that after the SDA won the elections, he would -- or rather, the Serbs when they marry would bring their wives to spend their wedding nights with Muslims. Many people were bitter because of there statement and that's why they considered him to be that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What about Fuad Ferizovic?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Fuad Ferizovic better. We did not agree about certain legal positions and things like that but I think that he was considered to be an extremist because he presented some kind of radical claims, perhaps in a political sense, this did not correspond to what people really liked to hear but I personally had discussions with him without any problems whatsoever. I don't have anything special to say in terms of my own appraisal of him. As for him being an extremist, I don't know about any such thing and we would really have to look at what a Muslim extremist really is. If somebody just says something a bit sharply, I don't think that he should be called an extremist. I know that he was in detention, though, his father told me that once.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to these people when they were locked up?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the rest but as far as Ferizovic is concerned, I heard from his father that a policeman beat him up in prison. Ferizovic is a person who has a bit of a big mouth, if I can put it that way, and possibly that is why it happened. At any rate, his father complained that a policeman had beaten him up and this man had been a refugee from Bihac. At least that's what he told me. As for others, I asked around after this detention centre was disbanded. I did not hear of anyone else having been beaten. However, all of these people are alive and they all know what had actually happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As far as the Crisis Staff was concerned, going back to that meeting of the 16th of June, they agreed to order those persons who were registered as extremists to be detained as well as those apparently possessing illegal weapons?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. That's the decision that was reached by the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then under the same decision, if you go back to that, there is the Bosnaplast being set up as a detention facility, and the SJB will remove all Muslim owners of weekend cottages from the Ostrelj weekend settlement. Why was that?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to these minutes, and this is simply jogging my memory, this was supposed to be in a big family home near Bosnaplast. I don't know why it was transferred to Kozila. As for Ostrelj, I believe that this was done because the command of the 2nd Krajina Corps, their officers, clashed with the municipal authorities in Drvar and the municipal authorities and the people of Drvar explicitly asked for the military to be sent out of their town. The military therefore asked for all weekend cottages to be emptied in Ostrelj. So Serb houses were emptied as well and handed over to the military for their use. As for the Muslims, this was probably for security reasons so that they wouldn't sort of spy on the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. You can hand that back now. And could have you a look, please, at P1834? Now, this is addressed to the Petrovac radio station. The position of the Crisis Staff is that radio stations should serve solely the needs of the present situation, i.e. state of war, the goal of raising the morale of the Serbian people, news, battlefield. All unverified information and unclear news which might result in the spread of misinformation removed. You should broadcast as many programmes as possible with text, music et cetera, et cetera. At this stage, did the radio Petrovac contain any non-Serb employees?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not before and not then. At that time, there certainly wasn't anyone there who was not a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And as far as you were concerned, did the Crisis Staff -- as far as the Crisis Staff was concerned, not you personally, was what the media put out important?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was considered to be relatively important because this radio station's programmes could be heard only within the town itself. It was a weak radio station. I personally was entrusted with the task of finding a stronger transmitter for it. You remember the case of Ciganovic, but it was considered to be important so that some news would not be broadcast that would cause any kind of unrest.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. It says the purpose of such programmes would be to persuade the Serbs in these difficult times when the war is being waged by forces wishing to annihilate the Serbian nation, that the people is the army and the army is the people. All programmes must be made in such a way that the Serbs understand they must fight for their salvation, freedom and territory. Was it your view that war was being waged by forces wishing to annihilate the entire Serbian nation?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what was believed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And to persuade the Serbian nation that the people is the army and the army is the people; was that important?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was important because this caused rifts between the military command and the civilian authorities, and the members of the command through the members of the military who went home often spread some kind of misinformation, along the following lines: That the municipal leadership was disloyal, not interested in the outcome of the war and so on and so forth. Therefore, the president, by way of the radio, tried to deal with these negative rumours and refute them, at least up to a degree.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. You can give that document back again. And now can we move, please, finally, on this topic of disloyal Serbs, I'd like you to have a look, please, at Exhibit P1837. Which is a minutes of the executive committee dated the 29th of June, and do you recognise -- it's a bad copy. Do you recognise the signature there?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The signature is of the president of the executive board, Mr. Bogdan Latinovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And there we see that pursuant to the law, and the Autonomous Region of Krajina Banja Luka Crisis Staff decision number 03531/92, the executive committee adopts the following: Worker Senada Medin [phoen], accounting department manager, is granted leave without pay from the 29th of June until further notice. Is this what you're talking about, about not actually dismissing people but granting them leave without pay?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Because if you look at the statement of reasons, we see, which is further on, the Crisis Staff decision establishes the obligation to remove from positions specified in item 1 of the decision all workers, et cetera, et cetera. Also for reasons of personal security, in accordance with the said regulations. Now, can you have a look, please, at Exhibit P688, and just confirm that that is the decision that's referred to? I think all we need to note is that it's got the same number that you referred to, Mr. Latinovic referred to in the executive committee, and it's dated the 22nd of June, and this document is dated some five days later. And then finally on this topic, could you look, please, at P1879? That's a letter addressed to the Crisis Staff with the subject of the implementation of the steps and decisions -- I'm sorry, haven't got it yet. Now, it appears to be Mr. Novakovic's -- it's his typed document but who did actually sign that?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I can see, it was signed by Mr. Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Okay. And that's a letter telling the Crisis Staff what you've done and you say or I'm sorry, Mr. Novakovic says the steps have been implemented in all public enterprises and in socially owned enterprises, all members of the police of Muslim nationality have been sacked from their jobs, employees of Muslim nationality were sacked earlier from their jobs in the municipal assembly administration organs. So judge, from what you say, are you saying that Mr. Novakovic was saying they had been dismissed when actually all that had happened is that they had been sent on leave without pay?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. You can see from this document that it has to do with a few workers who are ethnic Serbs as well. That's the criterion of responding to military call-ups.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And then the steps set by the Krajina ARK -- AR autonomous region Crisis Staff are in the stage of being implemented in the Serb Republic army units in our territory. Taking into account that not all staff could have been sacked from their jobs until they completed the necessary handover. All right, thank you. Now, that same day, and could have you a look, please, now at P1880? Did Mr. Novakovic also send a request for a special purpose police detachment to Stojan Zupljanin at the CSB in Banja Luka, although it's actually called the MUP here but --

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We have witnessed drastic violations of public order and piece as well as growing crime, curfews are still -- during police curfews a still unidentified group has been shooting, demolishing and looting taverns, shops and kiosks owned by citizens of Muslim nationality. But since recently also those owned by citizens of Serbian nationality. Mass theft where combat or cleansing operations are taking place or have already taken place, due to insufficient training or excessive tolerance, blah -- and so on and so forth, we are therefore asking you immediately to send one special purpose police detachment to Petrovac to bring peace and prevent the decreasing morale amongst part of our population. Was that an accurate description in your view of what was happening in Petrovac around the 25th of June?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a good, accurate description. That's exactly what was happening, except that I personally do not know of any attacks against Serb property, especially not any meaningful ones because I would have remembered that, this was simply added in order to have a political balance but basically it was Muslim property that was imperilled. That is why they asked for outside help because there could be no local intervention because of local friendships and various family ties and so on and so forth. They thought that if somebody came from the outside, they could even resort to force when attacking looters and plunderers. As for the rest, it is all the way it's been written here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And again, just so there is no doubt about this, do you recognise the signature of Mr. Novakovic?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise the signature, but also in terms of its content, the document is an authentic one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Can you then go, please, to your diary for the same date? Page 113, Your Honours. And I just want to ask you about this: You say 15th extraordinary session of the executive board today, implementation of the Krajina autonomous region decision. Are we referring back again to the -- about the decision in respect of dismissal of persons not loyal?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 25th of June notes? Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. It starts Slobodan Tadic at the top.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Yes. In these notes, under item 4, I wrote down a particular remark, that solutions -- or rather decisions should be drafted as of the 29th of June onwards, in terms of unpaid leave of absence, that's the document that we looked at a while ago because this name, Senada, this has to do with the name of the person who was given this leave of absence. Dinka and Omer are also Muslims, Dinka worked in the financial sector and Omer worked in the land survey department. That is as far as I can remember. I was not their immediate superior but as far as I can remember, that's the way it was, and yes, it does have to do with what we were discussing a while ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And during the course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you finishing?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just one last question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think you've already explained it but in relation to that decision of the Crisis Staff, as -- you gave the answer in interview, this is at page 82, that the letter that you got from the Crisis Staff or the decision didn't have the form of an order but it was obligatory, it was mandatory. Do you still adhere to that answer?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still adhere to that answer. That's the way it is. You can see for yourselves here, from these documents, that that's exactly the way it was. I've already said that a personal relationships vis-a-vis certain office holders were one thing whereas the observance of rules in terms of what had been established is a completely different thing because it would be very dangerous, for example, for the president or for the entire Crisis Staff if they had not accepted and observed the decisions that were formally binding on them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we will have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, very quickly, I will have lost half an hour today. Can I have an extra half hour on Monday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Cunningham?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I believe I'll need the full three hours or the full day for cross.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If necessary, Your Honour, the witness that follows we can complete even losing part to Mr. Cunningham but I hope Your Honours think that this evidence is important enough to take it in full.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For us, every evidence is important. Let's take it up from there. This witness definitely, I mean, is an important witness. There is no question about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wouldn't like to put any restrictions on you and on Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm grateful. We will just sort it out ourselves with the following witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, there was one more document I needed you to look at and I knew I was missing something.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's a new document, Your Honours. It's got disclosure 7.61 on it. I think the ERN number is 02933096.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I don't have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It was added in that little pile, the extra little pile that we gave you but we'll have it put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But my -- anyway, let's see.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's on the ELMO, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is a letter addressed to the timber processing company and again we are going back to the status of the persons of Muslim nationality. It's a later date -- document, the 21st of August. It comes under the signature block of Mr. Latinovic. Who actually signed that?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I signed it on behalf of Mr. Latinovic, and I also wrote the text following his instructions --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- after a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you enclose, I don't think we need to go through that but you enclose a copy of that decision we already looked at.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that be made Exhibit P2452?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Has the air conditioning gone off in this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I've already asked them to lower it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because it's becoming smelly -- it's warm and it's also, you can feel the staleness of the air. Anyway, let's continue, and in the meantime, Madam Registrar, please, could you chase whoever.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I asked them to turn down the temperature to 16 but it's not working.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm afraid, Your Honours, I have to go back to the 1st of June because I missed one document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you have please Exhibit P1867? Again, sir, these are a Crisis Staff meetings, the minutes, at -- held on the 29th of May, and I'll just check whether you had a note of this in your diary. I don't think you do. But, sir, again, can you just identify this? Is the signature on this occasion of the note taker on there?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is technical secretary's signature. I wasn't present at the meeting, that is what my notes say. I don't recall it at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was at a meeting that took place after that and again I saw it from the notes, attended by the commander of the 1st Krajina Corps and other army representatives but that one was the 23rd session and this seems to be the 22nd. Another reason why I think I wasn't present is that a decision was adopted which fell -- which did not fall under the municipal jurisdiction. That was the proclamation of the state of war. I don't think that one could ever proclaim the state of war at the -- at a local level.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: And you can't do it now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. And then you -- yes, because it goes on to say the military command and the Crisis Staff must reach a complete coordination with an aim to establishing control in the territory of the Petrovac municipality. And then item 2, the Crisis Staff has also discussed the situation regarding the emigration of some SDA representatives and has concluded the best solution is the said representatives stay in Petrovac. You weren't present, you say. Were you told about the conclusions of this meeting, though?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But I know what this is about from other things that happened. The SDA representatives who were councilmen and the MP asked that they be enabled to move to Bihac. I do not know if they asked for it personally on this occasion or somebody else but I know that the most prominent Bosnian Muslim representatives were transferred by Mr. Dragan Milanovic, and Dragan Ivanic and they did it surreptitiously. I learned it from another source but I think that is an accurate information, that is they were transferred by eminent Serbs, they helped them get out because there was a major risk of their being killed during all that disarray.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Why did the Crisis Staff, however, decide that -- make a decision that on the face of it saying they weren't going to be allowed to move out?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Yes, that's true. That was the decision of the Crisis Staff here and formally it was in force but this was done without informing the public about it. The public learnt about it only later. And I think that most of the ordinary people there do not know how they got to Bihac to this day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, you misunderstand. What was the reason that the Crisis Staff felt it had to say publicly that these people would not be allowed to move?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said it. The public pressure and especially the pressure brought by members of military units who came from Petrovac, who did it either through their commands or directly by way of some informal groups.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So public pressure wanted to ensure that the -- these particular people should stay within Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The public thought that they should be kept there, especially the representative of the military command, Mr. Vrzina opposed it all the time, and he always told us that that was what the army thought, but we didn't trust his interpretations because we could hardly accept that he went around and polled various soldiers on the front line, but they didn't want the eminent Muslims be allowed to leave. What they were saying was to keep able-bodied men and to let women and children go but we thought that that would mean that they would be staying there as hostages and that would be unacceptable for them and they told us explicitly that they wouldn't do that, they didn't want to do it, and we ourselves also knew that it wasn't possible. But since the formal Muslim representatives since they were representatives of the Muslim authorities or parties, there was a real danger that they might be killed because you saw that that whole Muslim family and those people were neither extremists nor disloyal and nevertheless the whole family was liquidated. From what I learned, the reason behind that was simply blunder but in so far as these other people were concerned, yes, their lives were in peril.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, you can hand that document back. Can we go back to where we were and could you look, please at P1838 which is the minutes of the meeting of the 30th of June? You were present at that meeting, I think, and as this is an AID-objected to document, can you confirm that this is an authentic record?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Looking at the contents of the document, I'd say that it is an authentic document, even if it is not signed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Very briefly, the political and security situation was discussed, and again, we are back to requests from soldiers for a more radical attitude towards the Muslims of Petrovac, that's in the second paragraph. And then the Muslims of Petrovac are behaving as if they were wounded and showing great fear. More of them should be arrested and isolated as a precaution, after which they should be given work obligations because there will be a lot of harvesting to do. Mr. Novakovic was saying that more should be arrested and isolated. Do you know why he was saying that?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of the pressures that came from the army command, Mr. Novakovic went directly because I think that -- I think the commander was somewhere in the area of the village of Radic, towards Bihac, and I think he went there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or perhaps he went to Vrtoce -- no, no, no but the command post was in Radic, yes, so yes, he went there and he is conveying the positions of that command to arrest them and put them to work, but when a work unit which was a proper work unit formally speaking to perform some jobs in that same area then those self same soldiers threatened those men with weapons and told them they would kill them all off. So the commander of the work unit simply brought those people immediately back to Petrovac and after that they didn't go out to work again. So on the one hand they requested a work unit they wanted people to perform certain jobs and when they go there to work then they are being attacked. So that in principle, these are pressures calculated to produce an excessive situation, that is if they do not meet their requests it's not good and when you do meet them then it's again not good.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Under conclusions until the prison in Kozila is made operational a plan should be made to arrest and bring in under custody all Muslims fit for military service who are thought to be capable of causing any harm to the Serbs and then the persons responsible. So this conclusion was anybody fit for any military age Muslim should be brought in, is that -- is that what happened?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, no, but able-bodied, those who could perhaps end up do something wrong, that is some people perhaps at whose places weapons -- on whom weapons or at whose places weapons were found and another group perhaps just were arbitrarily pin-pointed by the police or those army people. I do not know how they did that but I think it was done on the basis of whatever condition -- convictions that they may have been upholding at the time rather than on the basis of some reliable facts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we now, please, move to deal effectively with the movement out of the population? Could you have a look, please, first of all, at P1841? That's the 2nd of July of 1992 or rather it's a report of the previous day's meeting, you're present as an expert consultant, it states there. I think we have seen that earlier. What was your expertise, the legal expertise?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is meant is legal knowledge. We've already seen how some of the decisions, especially when I was absent from the meetings, how quite a number of those decisions are very questionable and quite a number of them unenforceable. My colleague, Mr. Sikman, is also a law graduate but at those meetings, he was quite inactive and he simply never said anything when people spoke lacking any legal grounds, he simply never commented on that. So that a decision would be made that would not be legal or lawful.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And in fact, you also recorded notes in your own diary.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is page 117 but I don't think we need to trouble to go to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In -- under item 1 the security situation, the -- it's assessed as a popular feeling of discontent especially directed towards Muslims after the recent events on the front line and stress that the best and sure solution for the protection of the Muslims would be to move the population. He emphasised the territory of the municipality was large and did not easily lend itself to safeguarding control. And then I think the rest of the meeting was concerned, as it's recorded really in your notebook as well, in connection with the medical centre and Dr. Vidovic, who talked about illegal profiteering and the like. So the suggestion there again coming through the army side is that there should be a mass or rather to move the population of the Muslims. Now, can you have a look, please, at 8 -- P843? 1843, sorry. Thanks. This is apparently an undated document. Could you look at it? Do you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is indeed Mr. Vrzina's signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, this is pursuant to a decision of the War Presidency dated the 31st of July, Muslims may move away voluntarily on the following conditions, they sign a contract on the exchange of immovable property and sign a statement giving their immovable property to the state, and it then goes on to talk about that. Do you know where the idea --

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- came from, that they had to sign a statement giving their immovable property to the state?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Basically, I don't know what the underlying idea was but from the very outset we knew that this decision was not legally valid. However, it was allowed to happen, in order to give legitimacy to the municipality, you will see in the concrete decisions in the statements of citizens of Muslim ethnicity that that's the way it was. Specifically, they left their property to the municipality. In this way, the municipality would get the legitimacy to protect this property from plunderers because we actually knew that there was a state of emergency on the situation was not regular, the people were threatened, that they were leaving the area. As for property, I myself told the president that it was the municipality that was responsible, that the municipality as a legal entity was responsible for the property of those citizens and that at any given point in time once the war is over, they or their legal heirs are going to raise that question and that they are going to set claims either for property that was destroyed or damaged. And as they would leave, our clerks would seal the houses and list all their valuables, regrettably even this did not prevent future lootings. Otherwise I think that Mr. Vrzina drafted this on his own because in a certain period of time while I was mobilised in a unit, they put me into this commission as a member, as a lawyer, and until I talked to your investigators, I had no idea that I had been a member of that commission. That does not mean that this did not happen. This is the way it was done.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. You see because it says at the bottom of this document, the commission for moving out together with the Petrovac Brigade command shall distribute immovable property given to the municipality. Do you know whether that happened? In other words that property that Muslims had to sign over to the state was given to other people?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This property was given to people for temporary use, temporary use. By way of a separate decision. As for the command of the Petrovac Brigade, this proves the continued pressure that was exerted by military representatives, and indeed, their soldiers who they appointed I think there were five or three of them on the commission, I know that it was an odd number, they basically said this person should be given some property, this person should not be given property, and then on the basis of that, the municipal commission would reach appropriate decisions. Mr. Sepa was in charge of this particular job but I know that I saw these soldiers on that particular business at the municipality all the time and here it also says that the revision of these contracts will be carried out. This is proof that people knew that these contracts regarding exchanges as a rule would not be legally valid. Because it had to do with one half or one-third, less here, enormous [as interpreted]. And I personally cautioned the president against that. They were cautioned, that inadequate property cannot be substituted for by a vast property. There has to be a balance. One has to strike a balance. So people realised this was just done proforma in order to make it possible for people to leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I want you to very quickly, please, just to look at P1844, 3rd of August minutes, which is continuing with the same topic. Just to identify, please, if you can, the signature at the end of the minutes.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a bit illegible but according to this last letter, the one that's been crossed out, I think that this is the signature of the technical secretary, Milka Jevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not going to bother to go through them. Your Honour, I'm just dealing with identification of authentic documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you have P1845, please? Which isn't on the list but I think it's important that we see the follow-through of all of this. Can you again just the signature, judge, it's apparently signed by Mr. Gacesa. Do you recognise his signature?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't see his signature often but I believe that this is an authentic signature, if it was copied from the original document. The letterhead and the general appearance seems right. It looks like the documents that they drafted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you see there is a stamp -- I know it's a bad photocopy, this, but there is a stamp on it. Is that -- what sorts of a stamp is that, at the top of it, I'm sorry, not at the bottom, not the municipality stamp.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the municipal stamp that confirms that it was received. That is one of the elements that I had in mind when I said that I believe that this is an authentic document. There are other elements that all point in that same direction but let's not waste any time over that. So it all seems to be right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And this document very briefly we can see that Mr. Gacesa is saying because the Muslims are leaving property to the municipality, they should find accommodation for these particular workers, the employees of the SJB. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And finally, please, could you look at 846? There are a number of documents there. Sorry, 1846. These are certificates apparently that were issued in respect of these people who wanted to move out. Did you see such certificates?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until I gave a statement to the investigators, I had not seen any such certificates but they are authentic because I know that forms were actually made for such certificates and that this was something that was being done.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We will leave it at that, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge, we are going to stop here today. We will continue on Monday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have a nice weekend.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Greetings, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: May I ask you in the first place whether you have thought about withdrawing this motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You haven't thought or you're not withdrawing it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I am not withdrawing it. I think it's an appropriate motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We think it is very inappropriate actually. I think that it's a last-ditch attempt again to disrupt the programme that this Trial Chamber emphasised must be adhered to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the last thing in the world that I want to do is disrupt --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're definitely trying to disrupt --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I made very clear, that we need enough time to be able to not only prepare the rule 90 -- decision on the Rule 98 bis motion but more importantly that we have ample time and sufficient time, considering what happened in other cases, to prepare the final judgement. What you are suggesting is to take us back three weeks, which is not acceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think I tried -- I tried, maybe I failed, I tried to make it clear in the motion that it is my very strong belief that by being granted the additional preparation time, we would be able to finish at the same time we are currently scheduled to finish. I'm not asking to stretch everything out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When according to you are we scheduled to finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My recollection, Your Honour, is that we were given 14 weeks and I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You were given more than 14 weeks, I gave you 16 weeks, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 16, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, if you are prepared to cut it down to 14 weeks, I am prepared to give you an extra week. And I am prepared to give you an extra week because we would gain one week ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Maybe I misunderstand. Are you saying that if I give you two weeks, you'll give me one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Don't expect me to treat you any differently than how I treated Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can give you up to tomorrow morning to think about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, what I said and I really feel very strongly about this, what I said was that if we are given adequate time to prepare the Defence case, I believe we would finish the Defence case in the time that has been allotted. Whatever the concluding date that you have, for the Defence case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not what I have. It's the concluding date that I have arrived at giving you -- allowing to you, irrespective of what may have been decided during the pre-trial stage because I don't really at this point in time, I prefer not to look back at the pre-trial stage and what may have been the opinion of my predecessor at that point in time, certainly living this case for more than a year and a half, has convinced me that while previously you said three months would probably be enough for your defence, now you're saying four months. I quite agree with you that perhaps you need four months and I'm prepared not to cut one single day on those four months. The thing is this: That those four months must finish at a date or on a date which would allow us what I have earmarked as the bare minimum, barest minimum, needed for us to elaborate, discuss, elaborate, draft, agree, disagree, and then come to the final judgement. And believe me, from what I have learned here in the past year and a half, I am risking a lot by earmarking what I have earmarked. I should insist on more.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me tell you what I'm struggling with, Your Honour. I think we are not on the same wavelength right now. I don't know what date 16 weeks down the road gets us to. That's what I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can tell you, the idea was for the Prosecution to finish by the 1st of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Then we agreed that you would have from the 2nd of August until the 22nd of August, time to prepare your Defence and file your Rule 98 bis motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's true, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then as you yourself maintain and rightly in your motion, you have got then -- there is from the 23rd of August to the 5th of September for the Prosecution to file its response. Then we agreed that since there will be a witness testifying late August, just one witness, testifying late August, I opened up to you and I said you will have an opportunity to file an additional note, et cetera. We have not established a date on that. We are easy. I mean we are definitely not going to quarrel or quibble on that. We were hoping and we -- I still hope that we would be able to hand down an oral decision on the rule 98 bis motion on the 3rd of October. Which basically means that on the 6th of October, you are scheduled to start with your Defence case, which is exactly six weeks after the presentation of, filing of the Rule 98 bis motion. I had earmarked up to the 30th of January for you to finish with your Defence case, and that's the full 16 weeks. Then rebuttal, rejoinder, if you want to give me the days, I can give you the days but I was working on those assumptions and basically it means that closing arguments on your part, final, would be 19th of March. This is the plan that I have in my mind and as I have jotted it down.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's the only thing I was standing here not knowing. What I tried to say and I apparently did not say it well, in paragraph 14, was that if we have that time that I'm asking for for preparation of the Defence case, we will finish the Defence case on the date that you just mentioned, that being January 30th or whatever. In other words I'm not asking to extend the back end of the Defence case by three weeks, I'm only asking to have time to prepare it better so that I can produce it more efficiently and get -- I can do it in less time, do it better, everything, but the time I'm given to put it together, the more I look at it the more I realise it's just not sufficient and we are going to have a just -- a comedy of stops and starts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No Appeals Chamber is going to like what you have just said, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm not talking to the Appeals Chamber, I'm talking to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I'm talking about the Appeals Chamber because if you force our hands we will have to hand down a decision. What I'm trying to avoid is having to say what I wouldn't like to say. This is what I'm hinting to you. I mean, I understand that you may have problems. I understand that these last weeks may have convinced you to take this stand, but as I explained to you, I have responsibilities towards the Chamber and towards the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe I wasn't heard. What I said was if I have this additional three preparation weeks, I still expect to finish on I think you said January 30th. I don't ask that that be changed in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. But you -- what you have not understood or forgotten is what I have been repeating throughout to you and to Ms. Korner, that when I say according to what I plan in my mind, we finish on the 16th of March, of 2004, and then 19th of March, 2004 and then we start our labours, I am not happy with that. I told you already I am not -- I know that I am running a risk, a big risk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] This is the position. I mean --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry. Giving you an extra week would not create problems for me if I gain something out of it. If I don't gain something out of it, I don't think I should. And the reason is that if -- the earlier we start, the earlier there is a chance that we finish. The later we start, the less chance there is that we will finish before the 30th, 30th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, what I'm obviously not saying well is I think that's not the case. I think and I say it in the motion, that if I have an opportunity to be properly prepared, I can move much more rapidly than if I am just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understand that, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Bouncing from pillar to post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But -- I wish I could speak more openly. Don't tie our hands because I would rather prefer that we sort this out now or tomorrow morning, not tomorrow morning, sorry, I'm definitely not coming here again tomorrow morning, neither Judge Janu nor Judge Taya. What I suggest to you is to consider about having an extra week but then giving us something in return. Because I mean, you are bringing up in your motion several matters, like as if you are expecting us to agree that the fact that this case started a year and a half ago doesn't mean anything, sort of -- that's irrelevant for preparing the Defence, that's not important. It's this -- from now until the next two months that is important, and it's your health that is important, which we acknowledge and we've tried to be as helpful as we could. If you tie our hands, we will have to speak in no unclear terms. I have already put down points now which I would like to sleep upon to tell you the truth because I don't want to be rash.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Judge, I don't know what to say. I think that -- I think that in view of the way other cases have been dealt with, in view of the complexity of this case, in view of the huge obligation I have to Mr. Brdjanin, if I didn't ask for time to be adequately prepared, I could be severely criticised for not providing adequate assistance to my client. This is the most difficult case that's ever been tried in this Tribunal. Other cases of much lesser note, as I've pointed out in my motion, have been given significantly more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I'm not --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: To prepare the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not impressed there and I can quote other cases where they were given much less time even with regard to the Rule 98 bis motion. I can quote instances where the Defence was given just seven days and the Prosecution seven days too. And it was by no means a simple case or more than one case. The logic of it all, Mr. Ackerman, and I'm going to close the discussion here, is this: You said if you give me the three weeks that I am asking, I will be better prepared and I can basically cut down my Defence case by three weeks because I would still finish on the 30th of January. Do you mean to tell me that if I give you one week, you will not be able to finish one week earlier?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: May be able to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So go back to your apartment or to your house, think about it, and come back Monday with some kind of response.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to -- I just want to show, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We don't want to be difficult with you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This is our average daily disclosure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you think you're alone?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I know I'm not alone but you understand it takes hours and hours to get through this. This is a sound recording of some kind, I'm sure, it's probably -- it could be as long as two hours, might be more, I don't know, it may be another copy of one they've given me, before, I don't know. But I have hours of these just to sit and listen to, I'm trying to put together a Defence case at the same time. I'm aware of the Court's problems with regard to the timing of this case. I'm not unsympathetic about that at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sure you aren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But I do want to fulfil my obligations to my client in the best way I can. That's all I'm trying to do. I don't want to disrupt this trial for one minute. I want this trial to finish properly. I don't want to have problems with this case. I want to do it in the best way I can. I want to be the best lawyer I can be for my client and the best advocate I can be for this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you sure are. And I hope --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's all I'm asking for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope this is also not meant to sort of proclaim in public, look my client is not receiving a fair trial because I would really hit back there. I'm promising you. What I suggest is that we sleep on it for the time being, and you come back Monday with my suggestion. May I also make something clear? And may I have the indulgence of the interpreters for a couple of more minutes and then we stop. When I say -- when I say start on the 6th of October, what we could do, we could start the week after, on the 13th, and in the week between the 6th and the 13th, you bring over those witnesses that are remaining that we had agreed will come forward before --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's what we intend to do. I was going to say we are going to start with cross-examination of Mr. Brown and Mr. Treanor. That's what was agreed. Not -- so in fact it's not really the Defence case as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just mention one more thing for Your Honours to factor into all of this. To let us know when you intend to hold a Pre-Trial Defence conference which is the norm?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And also to -- when you're going to require the list of witnesses, the witness summaries, and the Pre-Trial Defence brief?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Actually I have a meeting with my senior legal officer on Monday on precisely on these matters but his deputy is on leave yesterday and today, so -- and he is the one who will tie up on this. Mr. Ackerman, I suggest you think about it and we'll take it up again very shortly, sometime on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we maybe take it up Tuesday? I have some obligations on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. It's not something that has necessarily to be decided on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can we do a two minute private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session for two minutes. In fact, I wanted to tell you something in private session too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 1.57 p.m., to be reconvened on Monday, the 28th day of July, 2003, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24 25
